claims.text: Wear resistance in the proposed high-entropy-alloy coating has a non-monotonic relationship with ambient temperature.
Formation of a stable, continuous tribo-oxide film can reduce wear depth by shielding the metallic material from direct mechanical contact.
Wear performance degrades sharply once temperature exceeds the threshold for screw-dislocation mobility in the BCC matrix.
Increased screw-dislocation mobility causes rapid plastic deformation and oxide spallation.
The proposed coating initially has either a mixed FCC/BCC or single-phase BCC microstructure, potentially with nanoscale phase decomposition.
Dense oxide films containing Cr2O3, TiO2, and related oxides can inhibit oxygen diffusion in Cr-containing refractory high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Protective oxide formation competes with thermally activated screw-dislocation mobility in determining wear behavior.
Screw-dislocation motion in BCC refractory high-entropy alloys can proceed through thermally activated kink-pair nucleation and migration.
A stable, continuous protective oxide film dominates wear resistance at temperatures up to approximately 600°C.
The intrinsic ductility of the BCC phase increases with temperature because of thermally activated screw-dislocation motion.
Above approximately 700°C, dislocation-assisted plastic flow fractures and spalls the protective oxide film.
Oxide spallation exposes fresh metal to rapid oxidation and abrasive wear.
Wear depth decreases as temperature rises from room temperature to approximately 600°C because of oxide passivation.
Above approximately 700°C, wear depth rises sharply and the wear mode changes from oxidative wear to severe adhesive or abrasive wear.
At room temperature, oxide films are rough, inhomogeneous, and continuously removed, producing moderate wear.
The degradation boundary lies between 700°C and 800°C for BCC refractory high-entropy alloys.
At the degradation boundary, kink-pair activation becomes sufficient to overcome strain hardening attributed to the oxide film.
The critical transition temperature depends on alloy composition and the sliding-contact stress state.
Cr content affects protective oxide formation.
Magnetic-entropy effects and phase stability are not fully quantified under tribological loading at the proposed temperatures.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis places stable oxide protection primarily below about 600°C and predicts failure above 700°C, whereas its cited tribological record reports rough, continuously removed oxides at room temperature and 500°C but stable protective oxide coverage and decreased wear depth at 800°C and 900°C.
